title: Even with automatic garbage collection, why do memory leaks still occur in Java (long-lived references, unclosed resources, listeners, inner classes, poor cache management), and how do you prevent them?
shortTitle: Why do memory leaks still occur despite automatic GC?

s1_definition.profdef: A Java memory leak happens when objects that are no longer needed remain reachable from a GC root, so the garbage collector cannot reclaim them. Because collection is based purely on reachability, any lingering reference keeps an object alive forever, even if the application will never use it again. Common causes include long-lived collections that keep growing, unclosed resources, registered listeners that are never removed, non-static inner classes capturing their enclosing instance, and unbounded caches. Prevention centers on removing references when done, bounding caches, closing resources deterministically, and using weak references where appropriate.
s1_definition.analogy: The cleanup crew at National Bank of India only removes boxes that nobody holds a slip for. A leak is when someone keeps a slip for a box they will never open again. For example a clerk keeps adding every transaction receipt to a giant folder that is never emptied, so the folder grows without bound even though old receipts are useless. Or a clerk signs up to receive notifications and leaves the bank, but nobody cancels the subscription, so the notification list keeps a slip to the departed clerk forever. The boxes cannot be cleaned because a slip still points to them, so memory fills up.
s1_definition.oneliner: Java leaks happen when unneeded objects stay reachable from a root, so the fix is to drop references, bound caches, close resources, and use weak references where suitable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Java memory leak happens when objects that are no longer needed remain reachable from a GC root, so the garbage collector cannot reclaim them. Because collection is based purely on reachability, any lingering reference keeps an object alive forever, even if the application will never use it again. Common causes include long-lived collections that keep growing, unclosed resources, registered listeners that are never removed, non-static inner classes capturing their enclosing instance, and unbounded caches. Prevention centers on removing references when done, bounding caches, closing resources deterministically, and using weak references where appropriate.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The cleanup crew at National Bank of India only removes boxes that nobody holds a slip for. A leak is when someone keeps a slip for a box they will never open again. For example a clerk keeps adding every transaction receipt to a giant folder that is never emptied, so the folder grows without bound even though old receipts are useless. Or a clerk signs up to receive notifications and leaves the bank, but nobody cancels the subscription, so the notification list keeps a slip to the departed clerk forever. The boxes cannot be cleaned because a slip still points to them, so memory fills up.

**One line to remember:** Java leaks happen when unneeded objects stay reachable from a root, so the fix is to drop references, bound caches, close resources, and use weak references where suitable.

sections.s2_technical:
The root cause is that the collector only removes unreachable objects, so a leak is always an unintended lingering reference. The objects are technically reachable, so the collector correctly leaves them, but logically they are dead weight the program will never use again. Over time these accumulate and the heap fills, eventually causing an OutOfMemoryError.

The first common cause is long-lived collections that grow without bound. A static `Map` or `List` that you keep adding to but never remove from will hold every entry forever. For example a static list that records every transaction object for the life of the process. The fix is to remove entries when done, cap the size, or use a size-bounded structure.

The second cause is unclosed resources. A stream, connection, or session that is never closed can retain large buffers and native handles. The fix is try-with-resources so close always runs. The third cause is listeners and callbacks: if you register a listener with a long-lived publisher and never deregister it, the publisher keeps the listener alive. The fix is to deregister in a cleanup step, or hold listeners through weak references.

The fourth cause is non-static inner classes and anonymous classes. A non-static inner class holds an implicit reference to its enclosing instance, so if the inner object outlives the outer one, it keeps the whole outer object alive. The fix is to make the inner class static and pass only what it needs. The fifth cause is poor cache management: an unbounded cache is just a growing map. The fix is a bounded cache with eviction, such as an LRU cache, or soft and weak references so the collector can reclaim entries under pressure. A senior nuance is detection: you confirm a leak by watching the old generation grow across full collections and never shrink, then take a heap dump and use a tool like Eclipse MAT to find the dominator tree and the reference chain keeping the objects alive, which points straight at the offending root.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's audit component kept a static list and appended every transaction object to it for the whole life of the process, intending to flush it later, but the flush was never wired up. Over days the heap filled and the service crashed with OutOfMemoryError. This is exactly a long-lived collection leak, because the static list is a GC root that keeps every transaction reachable forever.

Problem 2 — The same service registered a balance-change listener on a long-lived account event bus for each short-lived request handler and never removed it, so the bus kept thousands of dead handlers alive. This is exactly a listener leak, and the fix is to deregister or to hold listeners weakly.

In the mini-project we show the leak and the fix. We define an `Account`, a leaky `AuditTrail` using an unbounded static list, and a fixed `BoundedAuditTrail` that caps its size and evicts the oldest entries. We also show a listener registered and then correctly removed. The demo processes transactions for Rajesh and Priya, demonstrates unbounded growth versus bounded growth, and logs sizes so the reader sees the leak and its prevention.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/leak/LeakDemo.java

# Run; a heap dump on OOM helps diagnose real leaks in production
java -Xmx64m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heap.hprof \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.leak.LeakDemo

# Analyze a dump with Eclipse MAT: find dominator tree + reference chain
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: 1000 audit entries appended to a leaky static trail, 1000 entries appended to a bounded trail capped at 100, and one listener registered and then removed.

Step 1: The leaky AuditTrail.record is called 1000 times. Each call adds a string to a static ArrayList. Because the list is static, it is a GC root that lives for the whole process, so every one of the 1000 entries stays reachable and the size grows to 1000 and never shrinks, even though old entries are useless.

Step 2: The demo logs the leaky size as 1000, representing memory that will keep growing with every transaction in a real service until the heap is exhausted.

Step 3: The bounded trail record is called 1000 times with a capacity of 100. On each call, if the deque already holds 100 entries, the oldest is evicted before the new one is added. So the structure stabilizes at 100 entries regardless of how many are recorded, keeping memory flat.

Step 4: The demo logs the bounded size as 100, demonstrating that eviction prevents unbounded growth, which is the fix for cache and audit-style leaks.

Step 5: A listener is registered on the bounded trail, then explicitly removed. Because the listener is deregistered, the trail no longer holds a reference to it, so the listener object can be collected once the request ends. The demo logs a listener count of zero, showing the listener leak is prevented.

```text
[WARNING] LEAKY AuditTrail size (never shrinks): 1000
[INFO] BOUNDED AuditTrail size (capped): 100
[INFO] Listener count after cleanup: 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  LEAKY PATH                                FIXED PATH
  static List (GC ROOT)                     bounded Deque (capacity 100)
    add TXN-0 ... TXN-999                     add → if full, evict oldest
    │ all stay reachable                      │ size stays flat at 100
    ▼                                         ▼
  size grows 1000 → ∞ over time             size = 100 forever
  heap fills → OutOfMemoryError             memory stable

  Listener leak:                            Listener fix:
    bus.add(listener), never removed          add(listener) → remove(listener)
    dead handlers retained                    handler collectible after request
```
sections.s5c_hld:

```text
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Service JVM                                  │
  │   bounded caches (Caffeine: max size + TTL)   │
  │   try-with-resources for all connections      │
  │   listeners deregistered on request end       │
  │   static collections avoided / size-capped    │
  └───────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Leak causes and fixes ═══

  Cause                         │ Fix
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  unbounded static collection   │ remove entries / cap size / evict
  unclosed resource             │ AutoCloseable + try-with-resources
  listener never deregistered   │ removeListener / WeakReference
  non-static inner class        │ make static, pass only needed data
  unbounded cache               │ LRU/TTL (Caffeine), Soft/Weak refs

  ── Detection recipe ──
  1. watch Old Gen after full GC: keeps growing → leak
  2. -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
  3. open .hprof in Eclipse MAT
  4. dominator tree → biggest retained set
  5. path-to-GC-root → the offending reference

  Rule: GC removes UNREACHABLE; a leak is an unintended REACHABLE reference.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Even though Java has automatic garbage collection, memory leaks still happen because the collector only reclaims objects that are unreachable, and a leak is always an object that is no longer needed but is still reachable from a garbage-collection root. The objects are technically alive, so the collector correctly refuses to remove them, but logically they are dead weight the program will never use again, and as they accumulate the heap fills until I get an OutOfMemoryError.

There are a handful of classic causes I always look for. The first is a long-lived collection that grows without bound, like a static map or list that keeps being added to but never cleared, because a static collection is a permanent root that keeps every entry alive. The second is unclosed resources like streams, connections, or sessions that retain buffers and native handles. The third is listeners and callbacks registered on a long-lived publisher and never deregistered, so the publisher keeps the listener alive. The fourth is non-static inner and anonymous classes, which hold an implicit reference to their enclosing instance, so if the inner object outlives the outer one it keeps the whole outer object alive. The fifth is poor cache management, since an unbounded cache is just a growing map.

The prevention mirrors the causes. I remove entries from collections when they are done, or cap their size and evict the oldest, which is exactly how I fixed an audit trail that was appending every transaction to a static list and crashing the service. I use try-with-resources so resources close deterministically. I always deregister listeners in a cleanup step, or hold them through weak references so the collector can reclaim them. I make inner classes static and pass only the data they need. And I bound caches with eviction, using an LRU or time-to-live policy, or soft and weak references so the JVM can drop entries under memory pressure.

One senior nuance I always add is detection. I confirm a real leak by watching the old generation across full collections: if it keeps growing and never shrinks, something is leaking. Then I enable heap dump on out-of-memory, open the dump in a tool like Eclipse MAT, look at the dominator tree to find the biggest retained set, and follow the path to the garbage-collection root, which points straight at the lingering reference. So my complete answer is that leaks occur because unneeded objects stay reachable from a root, the usual culprits are unbounded collections, unclosed resources, un-removed listeners, non-static inner classes, and unbounded caches, and I prevent them by dropping references, closing resources deterministically, bounding caches, deregistering listeners, and using weak references, confirming with heap-dump analysis when needed.

---

keyPoints: Leak: objects are still referenced but never used again
Common causes: static collections that grow forever, listeners not unregistered
Caches without eviction, ThreadLocal not cleaned in thread pools
Inner class holding reference to outer class (Activity leak in Android)
Fix: use WeakReference, bounded caches, explicit cleanup
